- 	that such repos need stronger stability/persistence guarantees,
- 	how updates to YANG are handled once the RFC is published (e.g., branch v/s new repo v/s same repo, do we create a matching new I-D vs changes in GitHub directly),

comments.author: dhruvdhody
comments.body:
I think this depends on what exactly is being updated:

- **YANG-only changes:**  
  If the issue is only in the YANG module (and there is no YANG embedded in the RFC text), then the RFC errata process doesn’t really apply. This should be handled via the VELOCE workflow (GitHub updates, module versioning, etc.).

- **RFC-only changes:**  
  If the issue is only in the RFC text, then the normal RFC errata process applies.

- **Changes affecting both YANG and RFC:**  
  In this case, an erratum should be filed and marked as *“Held for Document Update”*, since the fix needs coordination. The VELOCE process can then take care of updating the YANG in a future revision, while the erratum tracks the RFCbis if it is ever done for the RFC text.

issues.title: Proposed Workflow: Post-Publication Maintenance of YANG Modules
issues.author: dhruvdhody
issues.body:
_V2: Made changes as per the feedback, changes in **bold**:BC/NBC/Semver etc_
_V1: Here is a proposed workflow as I imagine it to work for updating YANG models post RFC publication via VELOCE_

----
# Post-Publication Maintenance of YANG Modules

This section defines how a YANG module evolves after the RFC that references it has been published. 
Development of a module that is not yet published as an RFC is unchanged: it follows the procedure in Working Group GitHub Usage Guidance [RFC8874], and this section does not apply.

## 1. Repository and File Model

A published module is maintained as a single canonical file in the WG SCM repository. The module name and namespace MUST remain stable across revisions; a change MUST NOT be expressed by creating a new file for the module.

Each change to a published module MUST add a new `revision` statement at the top of the module (Section 7.1.9 of [RFC7950]) following the revision-handling procedure of [I-D.ietf-netmod-yang-module-versioning], **carry a revision-label expressing its YANG semantic version [I-D.ietf-netmod-yang-semver], and describe the change. The revision date is the revision key; the revision-label carries the backward-compatibility signal (PATCH / MINOR / MAJOR).** Existing revision statements MUST NOT be modified.

Each published revision MUST be marked with an **immutable git tag named for its YANG semantic version (e.g., 1.2.0)**, or an equivalent branch that is not subsequently rewritten.

## 2. Publication and Locking

At RFC publication, the module is tagged and the RFC MUST reference that specific tag together with the revision date. The referenced revision is locked: the tag MUST NOT be moved or rewritten, and the revision it identifies MUST NOT be altered in any way. Any subsequent modification MUST be introduced as a new revision via the procedure below.

**Example text in RFC:**
> At the time of publication of this document, the "ietf-foo" YANG
   module is at revision 2026-06-30 with YANG semantic version 1.0.0 at 
   <https://github.com/ietf-wg-bar/ietf-foo/tree/1.0.0>. 

> The module is maintained after publication of this document following
   the procedure in [VELOCE].  Later revisions are published in the
   same repository; such revisions do not alter the version referenced
   by this document. The latest published revision and tracking can be 
   found in the  repository README at 
   <https://github.com/ietf-wg-bar/ietf-foo>

## 3. Change Classification

**This section is rewritten in V2**

Before a change is proposed, it MUST be classified on two questions: (a) does it require new normative prose, and (b) is it backward-compatible (BC) or non-backward-compatible (NBC) under [I-D.ietf-netmod-yang-semver]. The first question selects the path; the second sets the version increment and consensus rigor (Section 5).

Three cases:
- Editorial / defect, no new prose. A `description` fix, formatting, or a defect correction consistent with existing normative text. Handled in this flow as a base-module revision — typically a PATCH (no schema-contract change) or a BC fix.
- Small addition self-contained in the model, no new prose. For example, adding a TLV value or enumeration that introduces no new normative semantics beyond what the base prose already establishes. Handled in this flow as a base-module revision, BC / MINOR increment. No new Internet-Draft and no augmentation module are required; several such additions MAY be combined into a single revision. This is the preferred way to make small extensions, to avoid a proliferation of single-feature augmentation modules.
- Substantial capability requiring new normative prose. Functionality that needs new normative text and is independently useful as its own module. Introduced through a new Internet-Draft with its own module that augments the base, following the usual IETF process. VELOCE does not change this.

The deciding question for the in-model path versus a new Internet-Draft is whether the change requires new normative prose, not merely whether it is new functionality.**

Where classification is contested, the WG Chairs decide, escalating to the responsible AD if needed.

## 4. Pull Request Procedure

A maintenance change is submitted as a Pull Request (PR) against the latest published branch. The PR SHOULD be structured with the first commit adding a new `revision` statement (date and description only, no other change), the later commits containing the change itself.

The PR MUST be cross-posted to the WG mailing list. Discussion and the linked Issue record the rationale and decision.

## 5. Consensus and Approval

**This section is rewritten in V2**

Every PR that modifies a published module is posted in the Working Group mailing list before it is merged. The version increment under [I-D.ietf-netmod-yang-semver] determines the additional review and the strength of the consensus path: backward-compatible changes are the easy path, non-backward-compatible changes require a stronger one.

- PATCH — Editorial. Changes that do not affect the schema contract (e.g., description and comment corrections, formatting, reference fixes). Required: Responsible AD approval. These MAY be handled with errata-like lightweight processing.
- MINOR — Backward-compatible (BC) schema change. Additive changes that do not break existing implementations (new optional nodes, identities, features, TLV/enum values). Required: YANG Doctor review + WGLC + responsible AD approval + MGMT AD approval.
- MAJOR — Non-backward-compatible (NBC) change. Any change that breaks existing implementations of the published module. Required: a stronger consensus path — YANG Doctor review + WGLC + responsible AD approval + MGMT AD approval, with the NBC nature and its justification explicitly called out in the Last Call and recorded in the revision. 

## 6. Merge, Tagging, and the Latest-Published Pointer

On successful completion of the required approvals, the PR is merged and the resulting revision MUST be tagged **with its YANG semantic version**. The new tag becomes a published revision; like all published revisions it is then locked.

The repository MUST maintain a single "latest published revision" pointer that identifies the most recent tag completed under Section 5. Because a change reaches the main branch only after completing that procedure, the main branch contains only published, tagged revisions.

## 7. Repository Presentation (README)

The repository landing page (e.g., README) MUST clearly distinguish the following, so that an implementer who is not an IETF participant is served the correct artifact:

- Published revisions — a table mapping each tag to its revision date, the referencing RFC, and status (e.g., "frozen — RFC NNNN reference").

- Latest published revision — a direct pointer to the most recent tag that has completed Section 5. This is the revision an implementer building to the current standard SHOULD use.

- Development status — an explicit notice that open PR branches MAY contain in-review changes that are NOT approved for implementation, with a link to open PRs. The main branch contains only published, tagged revisions.

## 8. Ownership, WG Closure and Custody

WG chairs assign maintainers, which otherwise defaults to the WG Chairs. When the WG closes, ownership of the repository transfers to a designated home WG (OPSAWG by default), which continues to maintain the module under the process defined in this document.


----
_Disclosure: The idea was mine, and I worked with Claude to refine it and describe it here_

issues.title: Proposed Workflow: adaptation of the current process for protocol TLVs
issues.author: italobusi
issues.body:
In IETF protocols, adding TLVs after the base RFC (i.e., the RFC with the base protocol specification) it is possible, but not required, to publish an RFC-bis which obsoletes the base RFC. In many cases, an RFC which updates the base RFC (RFC-update) is published defining only the new TLVs.

The datatracker provides tagging to show whether an RFC has been update by one or more RFC-update or replaced by an RFC-bis.

Also bug fixing can be easily done with Errata and the datatracker provides tagging to show whether there are errata as well as to retrieve the text of the RFC with the verified errata inline.

I am wondering whether we can rely as much as possible on this process and focus on the adjustments that are needed because of the nature of the YANG language which requires a new revision of the whole YANG module when something gets changed

After the initial revision of a YANG module is published, there are three cases which might have an impact on that module:
- a bug is discovered (bug fixing)
- a new functionality needs to be added through a revision of that YANG module
- a new functionality needs to be added in another YANG module which augments that YANG module

I think that the decision about whether a new functionality needs to be added in a new revision or in an augmentation model is a design choice to be taken purely on the basis of technical considerations (e.g., modular design) and not being impacted by the process

From a process point of view, defining a new YANG module which augments an existing YANG module is actually the design of the initial revision of a YANG module and outside the scope of this issue which focuses only on the process to update a YANG module after the publication of its initial revision

A common assumption is that the base RFC will no longer contain the YANG module but a pointer to a stable repository (e.g., a github release)

We therefore have two cases left: bug fixing and new functionalities

## Bug fixing

A bug fix may impact the narrative text or the YANG module (or both)

My suggestion is to submit an errata for fixing bug

If the bug is affecting the narrative text, the proposed changes to the narrative text should be provided in the errata.

If the bug is affecting the YANG model:
- the proposed changes to the YANG module shall be provided in a specific working repository (e.g., a github PR)
- a link to that working repository (e.g., the github PR) shall be provided in the errata

The approval of the errata follows the existing process already in place for the approval of errata with some minor updates required to ensure that  the proposed changes to the YANG module, if any, have been reviewed and approved. The review of the YANG should only focus on the changes as marked in the working repository.

When an errata proposing changes to the YANG module is verified:
- the proposed changes to the YANG module in the working repository are merged into a stable repository (e.g., a github release tagged after the PR has been merged)
- the verified text in the errata is updated to point to the stable repository
- the verified text in the narrative sections, if any, are updated following existing errata process

An user of the base RFC can check the errata database (or the RFC with inline errata) to get the latest version of the YANG module(s) within that RFC.

## New functionalities: RFC-update or RFC-bis

The home WG can decide whether the changes in the YANG module revision are significant enough to justify the development of an RFC-bis or an RFC-update is sufficient.

We therefore have three cases:
1. RFC-update with no changes to the narrative text
2. RFC-update with changes to the narrative text
3. RFC-bis

###  RFC-update

An RFC-update may impact the narrative text or the YANG module (or both)

My suggestion is to submit an I-D proposing an RFC-update

If the RFC-update requires some narrative text to describe the changes, this text can be provided in the narrative sections of the I-D.

If the RFC-update requires changes to the YANG model:
- the proposed changes to the YANG module shall be provided in a specific working repository (e.g., a github PR)
- a link to that working repository (e.g., the github PR) shall be provided in the I-D

If the RFC-update just requires changes to the YANG module, the I-D can be quite slim: an abstract and an introduction briefly summarizing the need for the change and a section pointing to the working repository (e.g., a github PR) with the updated YANG model

The approval of the RFC-update I-D follows the normal IETF process (including the IESG review), with some minor updates required to ensure that  the proposed changes to the YANG module, if any, have been reviewed and approved. The review of the YANG should only focus on the changes as marked in the working repository.

Note: it is also possible to publish RFC-update to just update the narrative text of the base RFC (in case for example the narrative text of the base RFC has proven not to be clear or reduced to speed-up the publication of the initial revision of the YANG model). In this case, no YANG model changes are proposed and the RFC-update I-D will not provide any replacement to the pointer to the stable repository where the latest YANG model is available.

When an RFC-update I-D proposing changes to the YANG module is approved by the IESG:
- the proposed changes to the YANG module in the working repository are merged into a stable repository (e.g., a github release tagged after the PR has been merged)
- the text in the published RFC-update points to the stable repository
- the the narrative sections, if any, are edited in the published RFC-update

An user of the base RFC can check the RFCs updating the base RFC to get the latest version of the YANG module(s) within that RFC.

### RFC-bis

An I-D which obsoletes the base RFC (and all the other RFCs updating it) is submitted to the WG and approved as RFC following the normal IETF process (no big changes to the current process for updating YANG modules)

## Standard Conformance Considerations

A side effect of this process, which keeps a 1:1 mapping between an RFC and a YANG module revision, would be to address the standard conformance issue highlighted in:

https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/opsawg/tDYaMcVe-RCzYccJMCV90su3cDo/

## Items for future discussion

There are some open issues (e.g., which repository to use or how the PR in github are managed, considering also that github may be used by the editors during the development cycle). I think these issues are applicable to any other proposal and can be refined after the main direction is taken.

We can discuss at a later stage whether the stable repository is a github release or something else (e.g., an IANA hosted repository).

We can discuss at a later stage whether this working repository is a github PR or something else (e.g., an IANA hosted repository). IMHO, the key requirement is that this working repository should provide a diff compared with the latest revision of the YANG module to ensure that the revision is focused only on the proposed changes.

We can discuss at a later stage whether the initial revision or the revision in an RFC-bis should be embedded with an I-D (as in the current process) or a pointer to a working repository (e.g., a github PR) is preferable or allowed.

issues.title: Proposed Workflow on how to create and track issues
issues.author: mjethanandani
issues.body:
This workflow debates the discussion around 
- creating issues
- creating PR
- getting consensus
- approval of the PR
- closing the issue

When an issue needs to be debated, an issue should be created first, much like this one is being done. The issue should be described in sufficient detail to enable a discussion. It can be discussed in the bi-weekly meeting. Once there is a rough consensus on how to proceed, a PR can be created to outline the changes that will be made.

If the next version of the draft is -01,  a branch called v01 would have been created by an admin and made the default branch. That branch is called the "Version Branch". To create a PR, a branch should be created off the Version Branch. For example, if the PR is going to be committed to update the -01 version of the draft, the branch should be created off of the v01 Version Branch.

The branch where the PR changes will be suggested is called the "Issue Branch". The branch itself should be named "issue-xx", where xx is the issue number assigned to the issue by GitHub. All the changes in the PR should reflect the consensus achieved as part of the issue. Two approvers have to approve the PR with no strong dissenters before the submitter of the PR can merge the changes into the version branch.

Before the PR can be merged, all conflicts with the Version Branch should be resolved, and the draft should "build" cleanly. Once the PR is merged, and because the PR is linked to the issue, it will result in the issue being closed. It is up to the submitter if they want to delete the "Issue branch" at this time.

issues.title: Define the development lifecycle for a net-new YANG module
issues.author: mjethanandani
issues.body:
## Summary

All existing VELOCE issues focus on post-publication maintenance of YANG modules already published in an RFC. The development workflow for a **net-new YANG module** — one that has never appeared in any RFC — is not explicitly covered anywhere in the draft or in the existing issue set.

## Problem

When a WG decides to create a brand-new YANG module from scratch, the following questions are currently unanswered under the VELOCE process:

- How is the repository set up and structured?
- What branch structure is used during initial development?
- When does the module first receive a version tag, and what tag format is used?
- How do YANG Doctors review apply during initial development (as opposed to post-publication updates)?
- How does WG Last Call interact with the git-based workflow?
- What is the handoff point at which the "initial development" track transitions to the "post-publication maintenance" track (i.e., at RFC publication)?

## What needs to be defined

A documented **Track A (net-new module)** lifecycle covering:

1. Repository setup and initial structure
2. Development-phase tagging and versioning conventions
3. YANG Doctors engagement during I-D development
4. Review and merge authority during active drafting
5. The publication event: what git tag / release marks the transition from development to maintenance?
6. How the processes in issues A–N apply differently (or identically) to a module being developed for the first time vs. one being updated post-publication

## Context

This gap was identified during the analysis of the existing 22 open issues. The VELOCE draft should address both tracks:

- **Track A** (this issue): net-new YANG module, written from scratch, no prior RFC
- **Track B** (existing issues): post-publication updates to a module already embedded in or referenced by a published RFC

Without Track A being documented, a WG adopting VELOCE for a brand-new module has no process guidance for the most common starting point.

It has been popular among windows desktop people who either didn't have WSL, weren't allowed to use it, etc.  I find that Dockerfiles are where understanding goes to die.  Once there, nobody updates or ever understands what is there ever again.    
I read the text as I rebased it, I saw the RECOMMENDED (which means SHOULD) that we have some CI.  The text does not mandate a container, but makes it clear that some will want it.  I wouldn't have said anything myself.
Yes, the text doesn't mandate container only.  Aside: in many cases Dockerfiles don't need to be touched too often in they simply wrap the project (e.g., install packages specified in a .lock file).

I agree with Joe. The whole idea of using a containerized environment is so that the build environment is consistent across all the developers. Just having Makefile and scripts does not guarantee that we are all looking at the same environment. Just as an example, my version of yanglint might be 2.x, while somebody else might be using 5.x and getting a completely different set of errors.

A container has a high risk of growing stale in my experience.

If everything is just available to build the container (and as a
consequence, run it locally without a container) I'm good.

It might not be obvious, but I am also targeting the supply
chain attack vector here.

I have validated and verified the security of my (local) system,
and have trust in tooling installed on there. A container that
will be downloaded, or built, increases the review burden to
verify the supply chain.
